name: Rifle Green
lede: Rifle green is a dark greyish green, the color of the uniforms of British light infantry rifle regiments.

sections.title: A uniform color
sections.body:
Paterson ties rifle green to the uniforms of some 19th-century British rifle brigades, light infantry in a dark greyish green [1]. He names the Rifle Brigade of Wellington's army, which the French nicknamed *the Grasshoppers* [1]. The color was meant to blend with the countryside for riflemen who fought in loose order, a practical reason that is a reading of the entry, not something Paterson states [1].

Paterson files it among the greens, close to racing green and olive drab [2]. Our library has no earlier record, and the name's first appearance is undocumented there [3]. In printed English the phrase peaks in the 1860s and rose fastest in the 1840s, which fits a 19th-century military term [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch #444C38 is a dark, grey-leaning olive green, near [[hunter-green]], [[racing-green]] and [[bottle-green]] [3]. It is a common painted color: our archive of 23,781 paintings has it in 1,102 (4.63%), as photographed [5]. Most often it is a hidden color inside the painting, in 43% of the 708 works where it is found by lightness rank [5]. Sérusier is its most devoted painter, with it in 6 of 26 works, and Norway over-represents it at 2.4 times the expectation [5]. Because dark greens sink into shadows and aged varnish, these are look-alikes, not a pigment test [5].

origin.first_recorded: 19th century (uniform); name undocumented in our data
